messages.subject: Between group differences in covariance Graphs
messages.subject_clean: Between group differences in covariance Graphs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Just a "quick" question re. testing for for differences between the actual graphs rather than between measures. I noted that you have a section in the help file (section 7) about conducting vertex level group comparisons however, you make clear that you need the individual participant graphs to do this. I therefore assume that these functions are only viable for DTI-derived networks rather than those which use volumetric/cortical thickness data?

If so, do you know of  an alternative approach? I have considered that the same problem would be true of NBS package, due to the lack of information on group variance. Other academics have suggested calculating the difference between groups and the difference between randomly permuted graphs from each group, to see where the group difference element falls in the distribution of 'difference' between the random permutations. This, once correction has been applied, could provide an indication of significance for each element of this 'difference' matrix.

An alternative I have considered is the hamming distance, which would not provide a group edge-level comparison, but would provide a metric for estimating the difference between the graphs of the two groups. This would be similar to the mantel test run by the AOP function within brainGraph.

So I guess I was just wondering if you had any strong feeling on which or any other approaches, would be most appropriate for this? I apologise for bugging you with a question only loosely related to the BrainGraph program, but I have hit this stumbling block and with a supervisory team whose experience with graph theory is limited, I felt it  would be beneficial if I found someone with a bit more experience to brainstorm with!

Kind regards
Dan

messages.subject: Re: [brainGraph-help] Between group differences in covariance Graphs
messages.subject_clean: [brainGraph-help] Between group differences in covariance Graphs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,
I'm happy to discuss the topic. It may not be directly related to the package, but it is an important one to consider when you have volumetric data.

Yes, all of the content in Chapter 7 require subject-level graphs (DTI, rs-fMRI), which doesn't work with volumetric data (at least from a "standard" analysis as the one I list in Chapters 4-5). Similarly, NBS (Chapter 6.6) would not work for this kind of data.

There are a handful of alternative approaches. I have not seen anyone using Hamming distance, but some groups have used methods that are conceptually similar, so check out the papers below and their references. The "standard" is indeed to do a randomization test as outlined in Chapter 5.4 (either at specific densities, or by calculating the AUC across densities). This allows you to do between-group inference. Bootstrapping gives you estimates of group-wise variance, but again doesn't really provide information for individual subjects. Additionally, there are the AOP and LOO methods from Saggar et al., both of which are a part of the package (Chapter 5.9). I would like to eventually incorporate their methods of calculating the IC/RC towards various graph-/vertex-level measures.

Myself, a couple years ago I was trying to use the method of Leopardi (PDF: http://emis.ams.org/journals/ETNA/vol.25.2006/pp309-327.dir/pp309-327.pdf) which partitions a sphere into regions of equal size. I had the idea to apply this method to the spherical thickness values output by Freesurfer, which would then allow you to calculate single-subject thickness covariance networks. This has been done for neonates (see in PLoS One: Tymofiyeva et al., 2012, 2014; Ziv et al., 2013). Leopardi provides code for Matlab, and I had been writing code for a workflow to import spherical thickness data from Freesurfer into R, doing the partitioning in R, and then calculating covariance networks from there. However, I had to put that aside to focus on my dissertation. I may revisit this idea some time in the future.
Arbabshirani et al. (2017): a review article which is not specific to volumetric but has many references http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S105381191600210X
Wang et al. (2016): they estimated inter-regional similarity to create single-subject graphs http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/brb3.448/full
Kim et al. (2016): estimate individual cortical thickness covariance networks http://journal.frontiersin.org/article/10.3389/fnins.2016.00394/full
Batalle et al. (2013): similarity-based measure for GM volume (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1053811913008124). See also papers by BM Tijms and colleagues (2012, 2013), however those methods are based on VBM measurements and in my opinion are not as accurate as a surface-based method.
Kong et al. (2015): another VBM-based method of similarity, using Kullback-Leibler divergence. http://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0141840

Chris

P.S. The functions in the (new) Chapter 7 have not yet been added to the package, but I will be submitting the newest version to CRAN in the near future. There are also improvements in the NBS function which utilize what I have added for GLM's. I may re-organize the User Guide as well but will not remove content.

messages.subject: Re: [brainGraph-help] Re: ANOVA / GLM
messages.body_plain:
Hi John et al.,
I know this post is nearly 1 year old, but I have finally addressed the issues that were present in doing group comparisons. I hope to push the updates to both Github and CRAN in the next couple of weeks.

You can see the details in Chapter 7 of the User Guide (https://www.dropbox.com/s/wmupawb39bcdho3/brainGraph_UserGuide.pdf?dl=0). The examples are meant to be similar to FSL's GLM page, showing design matrix setup.

You will be able to do a 2-way ANOVA but unfortunately I currently do not have working code for a 3-way ANOVA. However this functionality is already greatly improved over previous versions.

Chris

On Monday, April 11, 2016 at 9:08:24 AM UTC-5, Chris Watson wrote:

> If you don't have any covariates, then you can use "kruskal.test" to test for a difference between all groups. I think the easiest way would be to have a data.table of your network measures of interest (in my User Guide, I usually call it something like "dt.net.meas").
>
> If, for example, you would like to test for a between-group difference in "vertex degree" at every vertex (region), something like this should work:
>
> dt.net.meas[, kruskal.test(degree ~ as.numeric(Group))$p.value, by=region]
>
> If you have multiple thresholds/densities,
> dt.net.meas[, kruskal.test(degree ~ as.numeric(Group))$p.value, by=.(threshold, region)]
>
> Note that this code only returns the p-values.
>
> Let me know if this helps you.
> Chris

messages.subject: Re: [brainGraph-help] Figure 22 in BrainGraph help guide...
messages.body_plain:
Thank you, I am glad they are helpful. That specific plot is from the function "plot_corr_mat". The code can be found in the block on page 44 in Chapter 5.10.1. It is the 4th command in the block, specifically:
plot_corr_mat(corrs[[2]][[10]]$r.thresh, type='lobe', g=g[[2]][[10]], group=groups[2])

1. The first arguments is the thresholded (binarized) adjacency matrix for group 2, threshold/density 10
2. The second argument is the "type" of vertex attribute to color the cells by. In this case I chose "lobe". Other options are "comm" and "comm.wt" (for unweighted and weighted community membership) and "network" (which only works for the "dosenbach160" atlas that has a "network" attribute, e.g. default mode, sensorimotor, etc.).
3. The third argument is the associated graph, here for group 2 & threshold/density 10. It is required to get those vertex attributes.
4. The fourth argument is optional and is what places "Patient" in the title; i.e., it is the group name. You could also leave this blank and then add your own title if you wish, e.g.,
plot_corr_mat(corrs[[2]][[10]]$r.thresh, type='lobe', g=g[[2]][[10]]) + labs(title='My Group')

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Try the following code and see the attached figures. Figs 1-2 are from the first ggplot command, and Figs 3-4 are the second.

corrs.m <- setDT(melt(corrs[[1]][[1]]$R))
corrs.m[Var1 == Var2, value := 0]

ggplot(corrs.m, aes(x=Var1, y=Var2, fill=value)) + geom_tile() + scale_fill_gradient2(low='blue', high='red', midpoint=0, limits=c(-1, 1), name='Correlation\ncoefficient')
Or:
ggplot(corrs.m, aes(x=Var1, y=Var2, fill=value)) + geom_tile() + scale_fill_gradient(low='yellow', high='red', limits=c(-1, 1), name='Correlation\ncoefficient')

You may also try each of the above after removing "limits=c(-1, 1)". These are in Figures 2 and 4. Let me know if this was what you were looking for.
Chris

messages.body_plain:
There are other color scales (called "palettes" in R) that you can investigate yourself. Or you can play around with different "high" and "low" values.
You can do a search for e.g.
* R color palette ggplot2
* R ggplot2 heatmap rainbow    # "rainbow" is the name of one of the color palettes
* R ggplot2 geom_tile palette    # "geom_tile" is the "geometry" function of ggplot2 that plots a matrix in the way you want it

and so on.

Chris
